Used heavily in math, code, and instruction tuning. 3) Aggressive filtering: select higher-quality tokens (e.g., domain-specific corpora, expert-curated content). 4) Multimodal expansion: use code, images, audio to extend the effective token budget. 5) Active learning: identify which training data adds the most value. Frontier labs use combinations.
pitfalls: Synthetic data can collapse the data distribution — training on AI-generated outputs gradually narrows the model's coverage. Repeated-epoch training has diminishing returns; past 3-4 epochs, returns vanish. Quality filtering is hard to do at scale without introducing bias (filtering for 'clean' text often removes useful diversity). Don't assume you can endlessly synthesize your way to better models — empirical limits exist.
when: Plan for data-constrained scaling whenever your team is training at frontier scale. Invest in data pipelines, synthetic data quality, and filtering as much as in compute. For smaller-scale teams, this is less urgent — there's still plenty of public data for sub-frontier training.

faq.q: Have we actually run out of training data?
faq.a: Not literally — but high-quality English internet text is largely consumed. Multilingual, multimodal, and domain-specific corpora still have headroom but are harder to exploit cleanly.

faq.q: Does synthetic data work?
faq.a: Yes for many domains (code, math, instructions). Carefully — model collapse from over-reliance on AI-generated data is documented. Mix with real data and validate continuously.

faq.q: How many epochs are useful?
faq.a: Empirically, 3-4 epochs are productive in data-constrained regimes; beyond that, returns vanish. Below Chinchilla-optimal compute, more epochs help less than more tokens.

title: Loss Scaling
short_definition: A mixed-precision training technique that multiplies the loss by a large constant before backpropagation to prevent gradient underflow in fp16 — keeps small gradients representable in low-precision formats.
full_explanation: Training in mixed precision (fp16 weights and activations, fp32 master copies) is much faster but introduces a numerical problem: gradients can become very small — sometimes smaller than fp16 can represent (about 1e-5). These gradients underflow to exactly zero, meaning some weights stop updating. Loss scaling fixes this by multiplying the loss by a large constant (typically 2^16 = 65536) before backprop. Gradients are scaled up by the same factor, no longer underflowing. Before applying them in the optimizer step, divide back by the scale. The training math is unchanged; numerical stability is restored. Forward pass produces a loss in fp32. Multiply loss by scale factor S (often dynamic, adjusting up if no overflow occurs and down if overflow does). Backprop with the scaled loss — gradients are also scaled by S. Check gradients for overflow (NaN or Inf): if any, skip the optimizer step and halve S. If no overflow, divide gradients by S and apply optimizer update normally. Dynamic loss scaling (the standard in PyTorch's torch.cuda.amp.GradScaler) adjusts S automatically to stay in the largest safe range.
why_it_matters: Mixed-precision training is the foundation of modern large-scale training — 2-3x faster than fp32 with comparable quality when done correctly. Loss scaling makes this possible by handling the numerical edge cases that would otherwise cause training to silently degrade as gradients underflow. Without dynamic loss scaling, mixed-precision training was a delicate art; with it, it's routine.
example: Training Llama-3-class models in bf16/fp16 without loss scaling: gradients for certain layers (especially deep within the model) consistently underflow to zero, causing weights to stagnate. With dynamic loss scaling (initialized at 2^15, adjusted as needed): gradients remain representable, training proceeds normally, final model quality matches fp32-trained equivalents. Wall-clock training time is 2-3x faster than fp32.
tldr: Loss scaling multiplies the loss before backpropagation, then unscales gradients before the optimizer step. Prevents fp16 gradients from underflowing to zero. Essential for stable mixed-precision training; usually handled automatically by frameworks (apex, torch.cuda.amp).

pitfalls: Static loss scaling (fixed S) can either underflow on hard-to-fit gradients or constantly overflow on easy ones. Always use dynamic loss scaling unless you know your dynamics very well. bf16 (vs fp16) has wider dynamic range and often doesn't need loss scaling — many recent training pipelines drop loss scaling when training in bf16 on Ampere/Hopper GPUs. Loss scaling combined with gradient checkpointing requires careful interaction (recomputed gradients should re-apply scaling).
when: Use loss scaling automatically via your framework's mixed-precision support (torch.cuda.amp.GradScaler, NVIDIA Apex). Skip when training in bf16 unless gradients are very small. Manual implementation is rarely needed; framework defaults are robust.

faq.q: Is loss scaling needed in bf16?
faq.a: Usually no — bf16 has 8-bit exponent (vs fp16's 5-bit), so its dynamic range covers most gradient magnitudes natively. fp16 needs loss scaling; bf16 typically doesn't.

faq.q: How is loss scaling different from gradient scaling?
faq.a: They're the same thing — 'loss scaling' is the technique, 'gradient scaling' is the effect. PyTorch calls the API GradScaler; NVIDIA calls it loss scaling. Same operation.

faq.q: Does loss scaling affect convergence?
faq.a: No — the scaled and unscaled gradients produce identical optimizer updates when correctly implemented. Loss scaling is a numerical workaround, not a training-dynamics change.

title: InfiniBand RDMA
short_definition: A high-bandwidth, low-latency network interconnect with hardware-accelerated remote direct memory access — the standard fabric connecting GPUs across nodes in large training clusters.
full_explanation: Training a 70B+ model takes many nodes (each holding 8 GPUs) coordinating tightly. Standard Ethernet has too much latency and overhead for this — every gradient sync would block the GPUs waiting. InfiniBand with RDMA solves this by letting GPUs in different nodes copy data into each other's memory directly, without involving the CPU or operating system kernel. The result is sub-microsecond cross-node communication that keeps the training pipeline saturated. Every major AI training cluster (NVIDIA DGX SuperPOD, Meta's training clusters, all major cloud GPU offerings) uses InfiniBand or RoCE (a similar protocol over Ethernet). InfiniBand is a fabric — a switched network with its own physical and protocol layers. Each node has a Host Channel Adapter (HCA) that bypasses the OS networking stack. RDMA operations let one node specify 'copy X bytes from address A on remote node N to address B on local node L' — the HCAs negotiate directly, the data moves with no CPU involvement on either side. NVIDIA GPUDirect RDMA extends this to GPU memory: GPU-to-GPU memory transfers across nodes without ever touching CPU memory. Communication libraries like NCCL build on top to implement collective operations (all-reduce, broadcast) optimized for the topology.
why_it_matters: Distributed training is comm-heavy: gradient all-reduces happen at every step. At Ethernet's microsecond-plus latencies, you can't hide this behind compute. InfiniBand's sub-microsecond latency makes large-scale training feasible. The difference between InfiniBand and 10GbE Ethernet on a 256-GPU job is often 3-10x training throughput — the bottleneck is comm, not compute.
example: Llama-2-70B training: ~2000 H100s connected by InfiniBand HDR (200 Gbps per port, full bisection bandwidth). All-reduce of model gradients per step takes ~3-5ms. Same job over equivalent Ethernet (no RDMA): all-reduce takes 30+ms, dominating step time and cutting throughput by ~5x. InfiniBand is not a luxury for large training — it's the difference between feasible and impractical.
tldr: InfiniBand with RDMA lets GPUs in different nodes read/write each other's memory directly, bypassing the CPU. 200-400 Gbps bandwidth, microsecond latency. Essential for multi-node training; without it, large-scale distributed training is impractically slow.

faq.q: What's the difference between InfiniBand and RoCE?
faq.a: InfiniBand is the native fabric protocol. RoCE (RDMA over Converged Ethernet) runs the same RDMA primitives over standard Ethernet hardware. Performance is similar at the top tiers; InfiniBand has lower overhead and more deterministic latency. RoCE is cheaper to deploy on existing Ethernet infrastructure.

faq.q: Do consumer GPUs support GPUDirect RDMA?
faq.a: Mostly no — it's a datacenter-class feature. Consumer cards (RTX) don't support it. Workstation/datacenter cards (A100, H100, H200) do.

faq.q: Can I do distributed training over standard Ethernet?
faq.a: Yes for small jobs (2-8 nodes) and patience. For large-scale training, the bandwidth penalty makes it impractical — invest in InfiniBand or RoCE.

title: ZeRO Optimizer
short_definition: DeepSpeed's family of memory-saving optimizer-state shardings (ZeRO-1, ZeRO-2, ZeRO-3) that distribute Adam moments, gradients, and weights across data-parallel ranks — enables training models too large for any single GPU.
full_explanation: Standard data parallelism replicates the entire model on every GPU and splits the batch. Memory cost is duplicated — every GPU holds full weights, full gradients, and full optimizer state (Adam's m and v buffers, each as large as the weights). For a 70B model that's 280GB per GPU just for optimizer state. ZeRO splits this: each GPU only holds 1/N of the optimizer state, gradients, or weights (depending on ZeRO stage). When a layer needs full weights, they're gathered just-in-time and discarded after use. Memory drops dramatically, communication increases moderately, training fits where it wouldn't before. Three stages of increasing aggressiveness. ZeRO-1 (P_os): shard optimizer state across data-parallel ranks. Gradients still replicated. Each rank only computes optimizer step on its 1/N. Memory savings ~75% of optimizer state. ZeRO-2 (P_os+g): also shard gradients. Each rank only reduces and stores its gradient slice. Additional ~50% savings on gradient memory. ZeRO-3 (P_os+g+p): also shard weights. Each rank holds 1/N of weights. Before computing each layer's forward pass, gather the layer's weights from all ranks (all-gather), use them, then discard. Memory savings approach single-GPU-only memory, comparable to tensor parallelism but using only data-parallel communication patterns.
why_it_matters: ZeRO enables training models far larger than any single GPU can hold, using only data-parallel communication (all-reduce / all-gather) — no specialized model parallelism or pipeline parallelism. The trade-off is more bandwidth on the data-parallel fabric, but for clusters with InfiniBand this is feasible. ZeRO-3 has been used to train 1T+ parameter models on commodity GPU clusters that don't have enough VRAM per node for any other approach.
example: Training Llama-3-70B with naive data parallelism on 8xH100 (640GB total VRAM): cannot fit. Optimizer state alone is 280GB; gradients 140GB; weights 140GB; activations 100GB+ — totals far exceed 8 × 80GB. With ZeRO-3, each GPU holds 1/8 of optimizer (35GB), 1/8 of gradients (17.5GB), 1/8 of weights (17.5GB), plus activations — fits comfortably on 80GB per GPU. Training proceeds at ~70-80% of theoretical efficiency due to the all-gather overhead.
tldr: ZeRO (Zero Redundancy Optimizer) shards optimizer state, gradients, and weights across data-parallel GPUs. ZeRO-1 shards optimizer; ZeRO-2 adds gradients; ZeRO-3 adds weights. ZeRO-3 enables single-GPU-impossible models on commodity clusters.

The just-in-time all-gather of weights is a per-layer cost; many small layers (transformer with deep stacking) amplify overhead. Combining ZeRO with tensor or pipeline parallelism (3D parallelism) is powerful but configuration-intensive. CPU offloading variants (ZeRO-Offload) trade GPU memory for slower training; use cautiously.

For frontier scale (300B+), combine ZeRO with TP and PP into 3D parallelism. Skip ZeRO when one GPU fits your model — standard data parallelism is simpler and faster.

faq.q: How does ZeRO differ from FSDP?
faq.a: FSDP (PyTorch's Fully Sharded Data Parallel) is conceptually similar — sharded data parallelism — and partly derived from ZeRO ideas. FSDP is the native PyTorch implementation; ZeRO is the DeepSpeed implementation. FSDP has become the more popular choice in 2024+.

faq.q: Does ZeRO require InfiniBand?
faq.a: Strongly recommended. ZeRO-3 communication is bandwidth-heavy; slow Ethernet bottlenecks training. RoCE or InfiniBand needed for production use.

faq.q: Can I combine ZeRO with tensor parallelism?
faq.a: Yes — 3D parallelism (ZeRO data parallel × tensor parallel × pipeline parallel) is the standard for frontier training. Configuration is complex; tools like Megatron-DeepSpeed automate it.

title: Tensor Core Utilization
short_definition: The percentage of theoretical Tensor Core FLOPs a workload is actually achieving on the GPU — the primary metric for understanding whether your training or inference is compute-bound or bandwidth-bound.
full_explanation: Modern NVIDIA GPUs (A100, H100) have specialized 'Tensor Cores' that do matrix multiplications at massive throughput — measured in petaflops. But achieving that throughput requires keeping the cores fed with data and the right operations. Tensor Core utilization is the ratio of FLOPs you're actually doing to FLOPs the hardware could do. Low utilization means your bottleneck is somewhere else: memory bandwidth, kernel launches, CPU sync, or just inefficient code. Optimizing GPU workloads starts with checking this number — if you're at 70%, you're done; if you're at 30%, there's massive headroom. Measure with nsight-compute, DCGM, or the deep learning frameworks' built-in profilers (PyTorch profiler, TensorBoard with profile data). Compute: actual TFLOPs / theoretical TFLOPs * 100%. Investigate low utilization with: 1) Memory bandwidth utilization — if low (under 50%), you're not even fetching enough data; if high (90%+), you're memory-bound, not compute-bound. 2) Kernel launch frequency — many small kernels indicate launch overhead. 3) Synchronization stalls — CPU-GPU sync waits. 4) Tensor Core eligibility — only fp16/bf16/int8 (and now fp8/fp4) matmuls hit Tensor Cores; fp32 ops use slower CUDA cores.
why_it_matters: GPU costs $30-50K each; underutilizing them is a direct waste of money. A training job running at 30% Tensor Core utilization is paying for 3x more compute than necessary. For frontier-scale training where the GPU bill is $10M+, this is the difference between hitting deadlines and missing them. For inference, low utilization directly translates to higher cost-per-token. Most performance optimization work begins by identifying and fixing low utilization.
example: Training Llama-3-8B on 8xH100 with naive PyTorch: Tensor Core utilization 35%, bottleneck is small attention kernels and Python overhead. After switching to FlashAttention-3, fusing operators with torch.compile, and increasing batch size: utilization rises to 68%. Training throughput jumps ~2x; cost per epoch drops by half. Same hardware, same model — just better-tuned code.
tldr: Tensor Core utilization measures how much of the GPU's matrix-multiply hardware your code is actually using. 70%+ is excellent, 40-50% is typical, below 30% means you're bandwidth- or kernel-launch-bound, not compute-bound. The first metric to check when optimizing GPU code.

pitfalls: 100% Tensor Core utilization isn't a realistic target — even well-tuned code hits 75-85% because of unavoidable memory ops and synchronization. 'Theoretical' FLOPs depend on precision: fp8 has 2x the theoretical FLOPs of fp16, so the same workload shows lower utilization metrics when comparing across precisions. Don't optimize for utilization in isolation — sometimes lower utilization is the right tradeoff if it enables larger batches or more efficient algorithms.
when: Profile Tensor Core utilization whenever you're optimizing GPU performance. Use it to diagnose whether you're compute-bound (good — optimize math), memory-bound (different problem — reduce data movement), or launch-bound (fuse kernels). Skip if you don't have specific performance requirements; default frameworks are good enough for most non-frontier work.

faq.q: What's a 'good' Tensor Core utilization number?
faq.a: 70%+ is excellent. 50-70% is normal for production code. Below 50% indicates significant optimization opportunity. Below 30% — you're probably bandwidth-bound or stuck in CPU bottlenecks.

faq.q: How do I measure Tensor Core utilization?
faq.a: NVIDIA Nsight Compute (detailed per-kernel), NVIDIA DCGM (cluster-wide), PyTorch Profiler (framework-integrated). For continuous monitoring in production, DCGM exporter to Prometheus is standard.

faq.q: Are Tensor Cores used for fp32 operations?
faq.a: No — Tensor Cores are for fp16/bf16/int8/fp8/fp4. fp32 operations use slower CUDA cores. Mixed-precision training is what lets you use Tensor Cores at all.

title: MIG (Multi-Instance GPU)
short_definition: An NVIDIA feature that partitions a single A100/H100 GPU into up to 7 isolated instances, each with dedicated compute and memory — useful for serving multiple small models or providing multi-tenant isolation.
full_explanation: An NVIDIA A100 (40 or 80 GB) or H100 (80 GB) is overkill for many serving workloads — a 7B model only needs ~14 GB, so the rest is wasted. Multi-Instance GPU lets you partition a single physical GPU into up to 7 isolated logical GPUs, each with its own compute units, memory, and isolation guarantees. Different instances see each other as separate devices — perfect for multi-tenant serving, hosting many small models, or providing isolated environments for testing. Performance isolation is at the hardware level: a noisy neighbor in one instance can't affect another. GPU is partitioned into 'GPU Instances' (GIs), each with a fixed slice of the GPU's resources: a number of SMs (streaming multiprocessors), a memory partition, and isolated memory controllers. The H100 supports configurations from 7×1g (1-GPU each, smallest slice) to 1×7g (all-in-one, no partitioning). Each instance runs CUDA kernels independently with no software intervention. NVIDIA manages partitioning via nvidia-smi MIG commands; orchestrators (Kubernetes with NVIDIA device plugin) treat instances as separate devices for scheduling.
why_it_matters: Cost-effective serving of many small models. Instead of buying 7 separate cheap GPUs to host 7 small models (which doesn't even pencil), one H100 with MIG hosts all 7 in isolation. Multi-tenancy: cloud providers and internal platforms use MIG to give users isolated GPU slices without sharing. Performance debugging: an instance's compute is bounded, so you know what your code will actually get.
example: Serving 7 small fine-tuned models (each 7B params, INT4 quantized at ~4GB each) on one H100 with MIG 7×1g.10gb partitions: each instance hosts one model independently, no cross-model contention, total cost is one H100 instead of 7 separate cards. Throughput per model is lower than dedicated H100 (each instance is ~14% of full compute), but the cost-per-model is also much lower.
tldr: MIG splits one big GPU into multiple smaller GPUs at the hardware level. An H100 can become 7 isolated 'instances', each with its own compute and memory. Great for serving multiple small models without contention; not useful for training large ones.

NVIDIA manages partitioning via nvidia-smi MIG commands; orchestrators (Kubernetes with NVIDIA device plugin) treat instances as separate devices for scheduling.
pitfalls: MIG instances can't be combined for a single workload — you can't aggregate 7 instances back into one big GPU mid-training. Once partitioned, you commit. Memory partition sizes are fixed by NVIDIA presets; you can't get arbitrary slices. Some collective communication operations (NCCL all-reduce) work poorly across MIG instances — they assume a full GPU. For training, MIG is almost always wrong; for serving many small models, it's often perfect.
when: Use MIG when serving many small models with isolation requirements, or providing multi-tenant GPU access in a platform. Skip for training, single-model serving, or workloads that need cross-instance communication. Plan partitioning upfront — it's not dynamic during runtime.

faq.q: Can I dynamically resize MIG partitions?
faq.a: No — partitions are set at the GPU level and require driver reload to change. Plan workloads to fit static partition sizes.

faq.q: Does MIG work for training?
faq.a: Theoretically, but rarely useful. Training benefits from full-GPU compute and memory bandwidth. MIG carves both into smaller pieces — bad for large-scale training, fine for tiny fine-tunes.

faq.q: Which NVIDIA GPUs support MIG?
faq.a: A30, A100, H100, H200, and B200. Consumer cards (RTX series) and older datacenter cards (V100, T4) don't support it. Always check before planning architecture.

title: Parallel Tool Calls
short_definition: An LLM feature where the model emits multiple tool invocations in a single response, allowing those tool calls to execute concurrently rather than sequentially — reduces agent latency on independent operations.
full_explanation: Traditional tool-using agents are serial: the model emits one tool call, the runtime executes it, the result feeds back, then the model decides the next call. Even for independent tools (search the web, check the calendar, look up the user's preferences), each call adds latency. Parallel tool calls let the model say in one response: 'call search() AND check_calendar() AND get_preferences()' — the runtime fires all three concurrently. For a 3-call agent step, latency drops from sum to max: a 6-second sequential pipeline becomes 2 seconds parallel. Native API support: GPT-4 (since June 2024), Claude (since Claude 3), and Gemini all support emitting multiple tool_call entries in a single assistant message. For multi-tool tasks, parallel execution can cut total response time by 2-5x. From a cost angle, parallel tool execution doesn't reduce LLM calls but reduces wall-clock time, which matters for serverless billing and user retention.

faq.q: Does the model decide which calls to parallelize?
faq.a: Yes — the model emits multiple tool_call entries when it thinks they're independent. The runtime trusts this and executes in parallel. Frameworks can override with policy (always serialize, always parallelize within categories).

faq.q: What if two parallel calls conflict?
faq.a: Design tool semantics to avoid this. If unavoidable, mark conflicting tools as 'serial-only' so the model serializes them. Many frameworks support tool-level concurrency annotations.

faq.q: How is this different from agent-loop parallelism?
faq.a: Parallel tool calls happen within a single turn. Agent-loop parallelism (multiple agents running in parallel) is a different concept — each agent runs its own tool-use loop independently. Both can be combined.

title: Structured Retrieval
short_definition: Retrieval strategies that exploit document structure (sections, hierarchies, tables, metadata) rather than treating documents as flat text — improves RAG quality on technical content like API docs, legal text, and scientific papers.
full_explanation: Standard RAG splits documents into fixed-size chunks of text and ignores their structure — chapter headings, section nesting, table-of-contents organization, metadata. This works for blog posts but fails on technical content where structure carries meaning. Structured retrieval preserves and exploits document hierarchy: each chunk knows its parent sections, retrieval can navigate up or down the hierarchy, and queries can target specific document types or sections. Quality on technical RAG (API docs, manuals, legal contracts) often improves 20-40% over flat chunking. During ingestion, parse documents into a tree: book → chapters → sections → paragraphs, or API docs → modules → classes → methods. Index each leaf chunk individually but tag it with full hierarchy path. At query time: 1) Find best leaf chunks via dense or hybrid retrieval. 2) Optionally expand context by including parent sections (for context) or sibling sections (for completeness). 3) Optionally filter by metadata (only methods, only safety-related sections, only sections published after 2023). 4) Produce the final RAG context with section hierarchy preserved as structure. Tools like LlamaIndex's hierarchical node parser implement this directly.
why_it_matters: Technical content has structure that flat chunking destroys. A 'how to authenticate' section makes sense only with knowledge of which API version, which auth method category, and which surrounding sections. Structured retrieval preserves this context. For RAG over API docs, legal text, scientific papers, and codebases, this is often the difference between a useful and useless system.
example: RAG over a 500-page API reference. Flat chunking: 'POST /api/v2/users' chunk lands in retrieval, but the surrounding 'Authentication required: Bearer token' and 'Rate limit: 100/min' details are in adjacent chunks that didn't get retrieved. Structured retrieval: the 'POST /api/v2/users' leaf is retrieved with its parent section ('User Management') and key sibling metadata ('Authentication', 'Rate Limits') automatically included. The LLM sees the full context needed to answer accurately.
tldr: Structured retrieval treats documents as hierarchies of titled sections rather than flat token streams. Retrieve a section, expand to parent context, navigate by topic. Much better than flat chunking on technical docs, code, and well-structured corpora.

Tools like LlamaIndex's hierarchical node parser implement this directly.
pitfalls: Parsing complex documents into clean hierarchies is hard — PDFs in particular fight structured extraction. Header-detection failures can corrupt the tree. Over-expansion of context (always retrieving full parent sections) bloats the context window. Different document types need different hierarchy schemas; one-size-fits-all loses to type-specific parsers.
when: Use whenever your corpus has meaningful structure — technical docs, scientific papers, legal contracts, code, books. Skip for unstructured content (blog posts, news articles, chat logs) where flat chunking works fine. Combine with metadata filtering for high-precision retrieval in large corpora.

faq.q: How is structured retrieval different from hierarchical chunking?
faq.a: Hierarchical chunking creates multiple chunk sizes (small, medium, large) over the same flat text. Structured retrieval uses semantic document structure (sections, headers). The two can be combined.

faq.q: Can structured retrieval work on PDFs?
faq.a: Yes, with effort — modern PDF parsers (Unstructured, LlamaParse, Adobe Extract) recover hierarchies for well-structured PDFs. Image-only PDFs need OCR + layout analysis first.

faq.q: Does structured retrieval need a graph database?
faq.a: No — a flat vector store with hierarchy metadata is sufficient. Graph databases help if your queries are heavily relationship-based (e.g., 'all methods that inherit from class X').

title: Pseudo-Relevance Feedback
short_definition: A classical IR technique where the top-K retrieved documents from an initial query are assumed relevant and used to expand or refine the query, then retrieval is run again — adapted for modern LLM-RAG workflows.
full_explanation: Pseudo-relevance feedback comes from classical information retrieval. The intuition: a user's first query is often imprecise — they don't know the corpus's vocabulary. The top-K documents returned by the first query, while imperfect, contain real terms and phrases from the corpus that match the user's intent. Treat them as 'relevant' (the 'pseudo' in the name), extract useful terms or concepts from them, and re-run retrieval with the enriched query. The second query usually finds documents the first missed. Classical version (Rocchio algorithm): 1) Run initial query, get top-K documents. 2) Compute a centroid of those K docs in term-space. 3) Update the query vector: new_query = α × original_query + β × centroid_relevant. 4) Re-retrieve with the updated query. Modern LLM-RAG version: 1) Initial retrieval over user query. 2) LLM reads top-K results and either generates additional query terms, rewrites the query, or extracts entities. 3) Run a second retrieval pass with the LLM-expanded query. 4) Use the combined results for final generation. The LLM does the term-extraction work classically done by Rocchio.
why_it_matters: Short or ambiguous user queries are common ('what's the policy on this?', 'how do I set this up?'). Pseudo-relevance feedback dramatically improves retrieval on such queries by leveraging the corpus's own vocabulary. The technique combines well with HyDE (hypothetical document) and query rewriting — all variations on 'use intermediate retrieved content to improve the next retrieval step.'
example: User query: 'how do I set up this thing for my team' (ambiguous, no corpus terms). Initial retrieval returns docs about 'workspace setup', 'team configuration', and 'SSO provisioning' (best guess based on context). LLM reads these, identifies 'team workspace SSO setup' as the intended topic, runs second retrieval with that as query. Second retrieval finds the exact setup guide doc that initial retrieval missed. Final answer cites the right document.
tldr: Pseudo-relevance feedback assumes the top-K initial retrieval results are relevant, extracts useful terms or context from them, and re-queries with that expansion. Decades-old IR technique that adapts well to modern dense retrieval and RAG. Especially useful when initial queries are short or ambiguous.

Drift in the wrong direction creates 'topic drift' where the second-pass retrieval doesn't match user intent. Cap the expansion: trust initial retrieval if it scored confidently; only expand on low-confidence initial results.
when: Use when initial query terms don't match the corpus's vocabulary, or for short ambiguous queries. Especially effective on technical or domain-specific corpora. Skip when first-pass retrieval is reliably accurate — the second pass adds overhead without benefit.

faq.q: Is pseudo-relevance feedback the same as query expansion?
faq.a: Closely related — query expansion is the operation (add terms to the query). Pseudo-relevance feedback is the specific technique that derives expansion terms from initial retrieval results, rather than from external sources (thesauri, ontologies).

faq.q: How is this different from HyDE?
faq.a: HyDE generates a hypothetical answer without any retrieval, then embeds that for retrieval. PRF first does retrieval, then uses real retrieved content to improve a second retrieval. Different starting points; can be combined.

faq.q: Does PRF help for very specific queries?
faq.a: Less so — specific queries already contain good vocabulary. PRF shines on vague or short queries where the corpus knows better terms than the user.

title: Intent Classifier
short_definition: A small fast model (often non-LLM) that categorizes incoming user queries into intent categories — used for routing, eligibility checks, and triggering different agent behaviors per intent.
full_explanation: Production LLM systems handle wildly varied user queries — questions, commands, complaints, jokes, attempted jailbreaks. Not every query should go to the same expensive LLM. An intent classifier is a lightweight model (or LLM prompt) that labels each incoming query by category before it hits the main system. Categorized queries route to specialized handlers: 'support questions' to a RAG'd customer service agent, 'sales inquiries' to a CRM-connected agent, 'attempted abuse' to a moderation pipeline, 'casual chat' to a cheap small model. Each handler is cheaper and better tuned than a single jack-of-all-trades. Training: collect labeled query examples for each intent category (typically 5-20 categories). Fine-tune a small encoder (DistilBERT, MiniLM, deberta-v3-small) on multi-class classification. Production: each incoming query gets a label + confidence in milliseconds. Route to appropriate handler. Low-confidence labels fall back to a default handler or human review. Modern systems may use a small LLM (gpt-4o-mini) for the same task with zero-shot prompting — slightly more expensive but no training data needed.
why_it_matters: Intent classification is the cheapest way to add structure to chaotic user traffic. Without it, every query gets the same expensive treatment regardless of complexity. With it, you serve simple queries cheaply, route complex ones to specialized handlers, and gate abuse before it touches downstream systems. The cost savings combined with quality improvements typically justify the engineering effort within weeks.
example: A customer service product receives daily traffic: 50% support questions, 20% billing issues, 15% feedback, 10% chitchat, 5% abuse attempts. Intent classifier (DistilBERT fine-tuned on 5K labeled examples) labels each query in ~10ms. Support questions route to a RAG agent over product docs. Billing routes to a tool-using agent connected to the billing system. Feedback routes to a sentiment-aware logger. Chitchat gets a cheap small model. Abuse gets blocked. Compared to single-model handling, total cost drops 70%, response quality improves 15% (specialized handlers do their domain better).
tldr: An intent classifier labels user queries by category: 'support question', 'sales inquiry', 'feedback', 'spam'. Usually a tiny fine-tuned classifier (DistilBERT, MiniLM). Routes queries to specialized handlers, gates expensive LLM calls, and enables fine-grained analytics on traffic.

Out-of-distribution queries can be misclassified into the closest training category — implement a 'reject' option for low-confidence cases. Drift: user behavior changes over time; retrain quarterly or whenever a new failure mode emerges. Intent categories should be exhaustive and mutually exclusive — overlapping or missing categories cause routing failures.
when: Use whenever you handle diverse user traffic and want to route differently per category. Skip for narrow products where every query is fundamentally the same type. Start simple (5-7 categories) and add granularity as you observe traffic patterns.

faq.q: Should I use an LLM as the intent classifier?
faq.a: For prototyping yes — a single LLM prompt can label intent zero-shot. For production at scale, a fine-tuned small classifier is much cheaper (10-100x lower cost per classification). Use LLM when training data is scarce or category set evolves rapidly.

faq.q: How many intent categories should I have?
faq.a: 5-15 is the sweet spot. Below 5, you're not gaining much routing benefit. Above 15, category overlap and rare-class problems dominate. Hierarchical schemas (broad + sub-category) help if you need granularity.

faq.q: How accurate does the classifier need to be?
faq.a: Depends on failure cost. For non-critical routing (support vs sales), 90%+ accuracy is fine. For abuse detection (false negatives cause real harm), 99%+ recall on the critical class is the target.
